claims.text: Stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in a refractory multi-principal element alloy will simultaneously increase room-temperature yield strength and tensile ductility.
High lattice friction suppresses dislocation-glide mechanisms in the target refractory alloy.
The initial friction stress of screw dislocations is high at room temperature in MoNbTaW-type refractory alloys.
High screw-dislocation friction and the absence of effective ductility mechanisms cause extreme room-temperature brittleness in the target alloy.
Some refractory multi-principal element alloys exhibit tensile elongation below the machine detection limit.
A specialized thermal-mechanical route can induce stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates with optimized size and volume fraction.
Processing within the solubility limits will preserve precipitate coherence and avoid brittle intermetallic phases.
Conventional processing can induce brittle HCP or Laves phases in refractory multi-principal element alloys.
Coherent nanoprecipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
Coherent nanoprecipitates promote a transition from screw-dislocation-dominated slip to edge-dislocation or cross-slip mechanisms.
The proposed transition in dislocation character prevents premature fracture.
Coherent precipitates increase the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation glide.
Appropriate precipitate size and spacing permit dislocation bypassing or cutting.
Dislocation bypassing or cutting prevents catastrophic screw-dislocation pile-ups and decouples strength from ductility.
The SCCP-processed alloy will achieve a yield strength greater than 2 GPa and tensile ductility greater than 10% at room temperature.
Simultaneously achieving greater than 2 GPa strength and greater than 10% ductility has been a long-standing challenge in tungsten-based alloys.
HIP can increase hardness or compression strength while inducing an HCP phase associated with extreme tensile brittleness.
Standard casting or conventional aging generally produces high strength with negligible tensile ductility in the target alloy family.
The hypothesized benefit requires the nanoprecipitates to remain coherent rather than transform into brittle intermetallic compounds.
Cr additions can promote precipitation of brittle Laves phase in refractory high-entropy alloys.
